title: What have EU policy changes delivered for shark and ray conservation in Europe?

authors.affiliation: Dutch Elasmobranch Society

abstract_text: Two decades ago the situation for sharks and rays in European waters was pretty grim. There were no limits for fisheries on elasmobranchs and endangered species did not have protection. Many species were in decline or had populations and historically low levels. A concerted effort by conservationist around Europe has led to a substantial increase in protective management measures aimed at improving the status of sharks and rays in EU waters, but are we there yet? Have these changes in the policy landscape yielded a significant result in the ocean? We present an overview of EU internal laws and regulations that apply to elasmobranch management with a validation of the level of change that has been achieved at a species level with an in depth analysis of several measures to pin point where the key to effective conservation of elasmobranchs lies. We differentiate between management of skates and rays, which are traditionally harvested commercially, and sharks which, with a few exceptions, tend to by bycatch species in EU fisheries. We end with clear policy recommendations and follow up actions for legislators and, who knows, maybe even a song!

abstract_text: The shark fishery in Tanjungluar Lombok is one of the largest target shark fisheries in Indonesia. Fishers from this location mainly use surface longlines to catch pelagic sharks in the eastern Indian Ocean and adjacent waters. We used 20-year landing data to identify a possible decline in shark production due to the fishery. A daily basis catch data collection has been applied at Tanjungluar since 2014. This method provided more robust data and showed a stable catch pattern rather than using the sampling-based method applied earlier. In general, the total catch of sharks caught by the surface longline fisheries varied from around 300 individuals per month in the low season to more than 1000 individuals in the peak season. Two CITES-listed species, Carcharhinus falciformis, and Sphyrna lewini were dominant in the shark catch composition within the last two decades. The silky shark contributed around 20-60% of the total shark catch every month and showed an upward trend in the catch from 2005 to 2021. Interestingly, the implementation of either CITES mechanisms for the species or the national shark management program seemed to have no or less impact on this target fishery. We discussed some possible factors that may sustain the shark fishery.

abstract_text: Unsustainable catches, driven in part by illegal trade, threaten 70% of the 52 shark and 85% of 71 ray species confirmed or suspected to occur in Bangladesh. Reported landings of elasmobranchs from targeted and non-targeted small-scale and industrial fisheries have declined by half from 6,234 tons over the past two decades, while official exports of dried shark fins (combined with fish maw) spiked at over 2,000 tons between 2018-2020. There is growing concern about the harmful effects of overfishing these apex predators on local livelihoods, food security, and the national economy. CITES Appendix I and II listings of globally threatened sharks and rays have catalysed efforts to improve their conservation management in Bangladesh. In 2021, the Bangladesh Wildlife Act was amended to strictly protect species assessed as Critically Endangered or Endangered in the IUCN Red List and/or listed in CITES Appendix I, and to regulate possession and trade of species assessed as Vulnerable and/or listed in CITES Appendix II. Non-Detriment Finding assessments for four species/species groups, including 15 CITES Appendix II listed species, confirmed the need for improved interagency collaboration, monitoring, and trade transparency. These NDFs also highlighted the need to reduce non-target catches and domestic consumption and trade that will not necessarily be reduced through stricter regulations on international trade. Improved prospects for conservation management of elasmobranchs initiated through collaborative research, policy development, trainings, and educational outreach exemplify how CITES listings can catalyse institutional collaboration and empower government and non-government stakeholders to implement evidence-based conservation plans.

abstract_text: Despite being fully protected in New Zealand waters since 2011, significant gaps remain in our knowledge of nearly all aspects of the oceanic manta's (Mobula birostris) life history and ecology in New Zealand. This lack of data has hindered comprehensive conservation management planning for this globally threatened species; New Zealand's Department of Conservation currently lists the species as "Data Deficient" in terms of its threat classification. A focused effort to better understand the New Zealand oceanic manta population over the past four years has resulted in a significant increase in knowledge of this species' population dynamics and habitat use. Combining citizen science and dedicated research efforts, 618 verified sightings spanning the time period of 1994 to 2022 have been collated from New Zealand waters, including 103 ventral photographic IDs, comprising 71 females, 26 males and 6 individuals of unknown sex. Furthermore, preliminary findings from intensive field work conducted in 2021-22 suggests that New Zealand supports a significant and healthy population of M. birostris. Observations include extensive feeding aggregations of more than 50 individuals, sightings of heavily pregnant females feeding alongside subadult males (disc widths of 590cm and 300cm respectively) and numerous accounts of active courtship displays. Moreover, this population shows very low incidence of injuries (17 %). These initial findings support the hypothesis that M. birostris are resident for at least part of the year in Aotearoa New Zealand and likely reproducing there and suggest that this population may be critical in global conservation efforts to recover this endangered species.

abstract_text: Physiological processes influence the movement behavior of animals. Understanding relationships between physiology and behaviour can lead to breakthroughs in species' movement ecology but linking ephemeral physiological conditions with movement patterns has been an ongoing challenge. This is especially the case for migratory, free-roaming species notorious for displaying highly variable movement over large spatiotemporal scales. Physiological and biological variables, termed "biomarkers", can describe underlying physiological processes that influence movement, such as energy storage and utilization, growth, and development. Here, we aimed to determine the relative influence of physiology on intra-specific movement patterns of a highly migratory apex predator, the tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier). We accomplished this by analyzing 50 measured biomarkers for nutritional and energetic condition, metabolism, morphology, reproduction, and health, in addition to seasonality, on the dispersion and scale of tiger shark movement across multiple temporal periods (7 – 25 days). Overall, nutrition-related biomarkers had the largest relative influence on movement, followed by metabolic hormones, energy substrates, and morphology. Reproductive state, health, and season had negligible influence on the movement patterns observed across the temporal periods considered. These results emphasize the importance of tiger sharks acquiring, storing, and mobilizing energy to support their movements, providing important knowledge about their movement ecology. Our work presents a novel approach for addressing the challenge of linking movement patterns of free-roaming species to their physiology and has wide applicability for future studies investigating the drivers of individual variation in movement of highly mobile species.

abstract_text: Mozambique is a hotspot for threatened and data deficient species of sharks and rays, yet a lack of site-specific information hinders the development of local and national species management plans. The largest identified population of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) in Africa aggregate within a 350 km upwelling zone that extends from the Bazaruto Archipelago in the north, to Zavora in the south. An 88% decline in sightings of M.alfredi along the Mozambican coastline represents one of the largest declines on record. Using sightings and photo-ID data from dive surveys conducted during 2009-2021, we investigate sightings trends, habitat preference, and population demographics of M. alfredi in Zavora Bay. The site and seasonal affinity of M. alfredi in Zavora Bay highlights the importance of understanding fine-scale site use within the larger home range of this population to develop local management strategies. Our findings provide evidence that Zavora Bay is a critical visitation site for reef manta rays in Mozambique and should be considered a conservation priority area for this threatened species.

abstract_text: The sicklefin lemon shark, Negaprion acutidens, is globally understudied compared to its sister species the Atlantic lemon shark, N. brevirostris. Although it has been heavily targeted by artificial provisioning activities until 2017, its movements are still unknown in the Society Islands, French Polynesia. Here, we used acoustic telemetry to study the residency and movement patterns of the sicklefin lemon shark between June 2014 and July 2015. We deployed 21 receivers on the outer reefs of Tahiti (n=11), Moorea (n=7), and Tetiaroa (n=3), an atoll located approximately 50 km north of Tahiti and Moorea. A total of 17 mature individuals were tagged internally by ingestion or externally using a speargun. Preliminary analyses indicate that sharks were primarily detected around Moorea and at the Vallée Blanche, northeast of Tahiti, while no individuals were detected in Tetiaroa. The number of detections is higher where shark-feeding occurred during the study period and decreases with the distance from tagging location. Globally, the detections mostly occurred during the day, suggesting that adult sicklefin lemon sharks use the outer reef during the day and move to deeper waters at night. Therefore, the sicklefin lemon shark seems to be highly resident and could be impacted by artificial provisioning activities at a small spatial scale. Considering that artificial provisioning is now forbidden in French Polynesia waters, such data is crucial to understand the long-term impacts of this activity on sharks movements, and could pave the way for further studies focusing on dishabituation process regarding artificial provisioning in shark species.

abstract_text: The global trade in elasmobranch products contributes to dramatic declines in elasmobranch populations. Recognising realistic and context-appropriate solutions to mitigate trade requires a thorough grasp of elasmobranch marketplaces that are notoriously inadequate where products originate, predominantly in the global south. We assessed the market components of the elasmobranch fin trade in the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh, using a framework designed for wildlife markets utilising mixed-method approaches. We found that markets are supply-driven and complex. Fins are supplied from protected and unprotected species, targeted and by-caught, and traded with other fishery and elasmobranch products. We highlighted challenges due to no reporting, limited monitoring and the difficulties in segregating species/products of different legal statuses. An unjust power structure between low-access harvesters and high-access actors with finances, market information and social ties was evident. The discriminative power exercising influenced unsustainable trade by high-access actors attaining excessive and unequal benefits from the market and often impacting independent decision-making of low-access actors (e.g., adopting conservation measures). We found ambiguous clarity about legality, growing distrust between fishers and fishery managers/policy-makers, and confusion regarding the infrequent seizures resulting from limited awareness, acceptance and no collaborative approach preceding law-making and enacting. These led to increased conflicts, corruption, non-compliance and unwillingness to report catch. Actors' behaviours are driven by diverse motivations, requiring a sophisticated regulation for reducing catch and trade, with local and global benefits. We provided targeted management recommendations to mitigate unsustainable trade, e.g., sustainable catch quotas, better financial arrangements, improved access to incentives for low-access actors, and other market solutions.

abstract_text: Trade restrictions have been established to counteract the rapid global decline of sharks and rays. This has resulted from high fishing pressure, by-catch and market demand for certain products (e.g. fins). Tackling the illegal trade of endangered species poses enormous challenges for authorities, including taxonomic ambiguity, product variety, logistical issues for inspections and trade flow complexity. Traditional genetic techniques have been developed, but these techniques are either time-consuming or species-specific, and generally fail to provide a comprehensive picture of the biological complexity underlying trade patterns. Here, we explore a powerful, alternative option, based on the high-throughput sequencing of trace DNA fragments retrieved from dust and scraps left behind by trade activities. We collected 28 'shark-dust' samples from seven processing plants across Java, Indonesia, and generated shark and ray sequences through DNA metabarcoding. We also collected individual tissue samples (175) in the same processing plants and identified the species by high-throughput barcoding (HTB) for comparison. Over 74% of reads belonged to CITES-listed species i.e. hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna spp.), silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis), bigeye thresher shark (Alopias superciliosus) and the recently CITES-listed giant guitarfish (Glaucostegus typus). A total of 75 shark and ray genera (representing half of the chondrichthyan orders) were identified, with 20 more taxa detected using the dust samples than those identified using tissue samples. Furthermore, dust samples were shown to effectively capture the species diversity being exploited. We argue that this 'shark-dust' approach is likely to become a powerful and cost-effective monitoring tool wherever elasmobranchs are traded.

abstract_text: Cocos Island is known to have one of the largest biomass levels of predatory fish in the tropics, yet our knowledge of the drivers affecting elasmobranch abundance and distribution patterns is limited. This study examined the effect of spatial, seasonal, and environmental drivers on elasmobranch assemblages at Cocos Island using baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS) between 2016 and 2020. Elasmobranchs were detected in 95% of the BRUVS, with stations having on average 2.7 ± 1.6 species and 6.3 ± 6.5 ind/hour largely overcoming the mean relative abundance reported by BRUVS in other protected reef systems. A total of 13 species comprised the elasmobranch assemblage of Cocos Island, which was clearly divided between pelagic and benthic environments. Depth and habitat were identified as the major factors structuring elasmobranch assemblages in benthic environments, although substrate cover, distance to the coast and season were also significant predictors. Significant indicator species with stronger species-habitat associations were the silky shark Carcharhinus falciformis dominating pelagic habitats, the white tip reef shark Triaenodon obesus and the black tip reef shark Carcharhinus melanopterus dominating warm shallow areas with coral or rocky reefs, the scalloped hammerhead shark Sphyrna lewini associated with pinnacles at greater distances from the coast and the silvertip shark Carcharhinus albimarginatus with preference for deeper sandy areas in bays and inshore sites. This study represents the first attempt at describing ecological patterns of elasmobranch assemblages removing human presence from the water and using a systematic research survey in benthic and pelagic environments of Cocos Island.

abstract_text: Social and collective behaviours as well as group formation are found across the animal kingdom including sharks and rays. Animal aggregations may result from a common requirement for shared resources or favourable environmental conditions and are not necessarily driven by social attraction between individuals. Although they have been considered mostly solitary organisms, improvements in analytical tools and the technology used to study behaviours in the wild has led to the confirmation that many elasmobranch species were more social than previously thought and to a better understanding of the form, structure, function and ecological significance of associations and grouping in sharks and rays. abstract_text: Metabolism underpins life histories, population dynamics, and extinction risk. Morphological traits that are linked to an organism's metabolism may provide a first approximation to the ecological needs to support growth, survival, and reproduction. abstract_text: Devil rays of the genus Mobula are subject to fishing exploitation worldwide, the population's reductions are evidenced by a decline in the number of catches of these rays, for this reason, they are considered vulnerable to overexploitation. Limited biological knowledge on these species has forced the use of precautionary conservation measures in some countries where intensive fishing occurs. There is few information about the reproductive biology of these species. This study aimed to describe the reproductive activity of three endangered species of the genus Mobula (Mobula munkiana, Mobula thurstoni, and Mobula mobular) in the Gulf of California. Reproductive organs were collected during 7 years of commercial fishing (2001–2007), and data on population structure, sex ratio, gamete production, and the number of offspring per breeding period were obtained. Maturity stages were determined through histological analysis of the gonads for both sexes, and the size at maturity was estimated based on anatomical and histological characteristics of the specimens caught. According to the results, there is an urgent need to apply strict conservation measures, such as fishery closures during the breeding season (May to September) or the establishment of catch sizes after specimens have reached sexual maturity, mainly in the countries where these rays are caught.

abstract_text: Scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphryna lewini) routinely perform rapid deep dives to forage on meso and bathypelagic prey. These deep dives consist of intensive burst swimming followed by resting periods in the surface mixed layer. Swimming muscle temperature profiles suggest S. lewini suppress their gill function as a means to reduce convective heat loss. Such intensive swimming behavior coupled with supposedly reduced respiration raises questions concerning the aerobic and anaerobic metabolic capacity of their white swimming muscle. Measuring the activity rates of key enzymes used in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism provides an indirect indicator of the metabolic potential of a tissue. Here we measured the maximal activities of aerobic enzymes citrate synthase (CS), malate dehydrogenase (MDH) and anaerobic enzymes pyruvate kinase (PK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) from white swimming muscle of S. lewini and were compared to those measured from other coastal, deep-dwelling, and highly active endothermic shark species. Sphyrna lewini had significantly higher activity levels of LDH, an anaerobic enzyme, and MDH, an aerobic enzyme. Results indicate the white muscle tissue of S. lewini is highly anaerobic dependent for burst swimming but has a high potential for lactate buildup. High activity rates of MDH indicate the potential for lactate to be rapidly reduced under aerobic conditions such as those experienced in the surface mixed layer between dives. These physiological adaptations likely enable S. lewini to remain highly active while suppressing gill function during deep dives and thereby exploit a very different ecological niche from sympatric shark species.

abstract_text: Sharks and rays support many ecological roles in coastal marine ecosystems, however widespread overfishing and habitat loss have resulted in population declines. Despite the intrinsic vulnerability of shark and ray populations due to their life-history characteristics, such as slow growth, low fecundity and late reproductive maturity, shark and ray functional community structure from a trait-based approach has rarely been quantified. Here, we provide a global assessment of shark and ray functional community structure among 230 tropical coral reefs in 42 nations across three ocean basins. We find that socio-economic conditions mediate shark and ray functional diversity, functional originality (the uniqueness of the community based on their traits) and functional dispersion (the overall breadth of trait combinations). Higher human gravity is strongly associated with degradation of all functional biodiversity metrics, while the trait structure of highly populated areas favour benthic and invertivorous sharks and rays. Large-bodied, pelagic and benthopelagic, deep diving, piscivorous and higher order carnivorous species are less abundant under increased human impacts. Biogeographically, Atlantic assemblages are more functionally original and diverse than Pacific assemblages, which are more represented by traits indicative of reef sharks rather than rays, such as fusiform body shape, ram ventilation and pelagic or benthopelagic lifestyles. Closed marine protected areas support substantially higher functional biodiversity than restricted and openly fished areas. Our findings illustrate the large-scale functional degradation of shark communities on coral reefs but identify spatial management tools as powerful avenues for protecting shark and ray functional integrity.

abstract_text: Elasmobranchii belongs to an old evolutionary class of vertebrates that diverged 450 mya. These species present a wide diversity of reproductive strategies while preserving the ancient mode of internal fertilization. Moreover, many of them are considered endangered and may be extinct soon. Understanding the principles of sperm motility and sperm physiology is essential to developing assisted reproductive techniques for this species group. Additionally, it is also important from evolutionary and general physiological perspectives as a part of reproduction studies. Elasmobranchii species possess relatively big spermatozoa (compared to bony fishes), with an elongated spiral shape head and tail similar to one currently existing (but later diverged) in birds, reptiles, and amphibians, which can be considered an evolutionary ancient. These particular structures may be associated with the necessity to penetrate viscous ovarian fluid or the jelly layer of eggs, suggesting environmental viscosity as the driving force which shapes big-sized spermatozoa head to the spiral shape during evolution. In the present study, we observed spermatozoa motion by regular and high-speed video microscopy to visualize sperm and flagellar motion in three different Elasmobranchii species: the freshwater ray Potamotrygon motoro, the marine skate Raja asterias and the shark Scyliorhinus canicula. We investigated the effect of surrounding media viscosity on spermatozoa motility parameters and their ability to propagate, release from spermatozeugmata, and perform directional changes. Our results suggest that the surrounding media's viscosity regulates spermatozoa motility and may affect its performance during fertilization in the Elasmobranchii species.

abstract_text: The whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari), a large pelagic migratory ray with an endangered status on the IUCN red list, displays slow growth and late maturity life history characteristics based on available literature. Historically, its age and growth parameters have been reported through vertebral aging methods. However, the periodicity of vertebrate band pair formation, which is used for aging, has not been validated for this species, making aging accuracy and thus the resulting growth parameters uncertain. In this study, we used both a frequentist and Bayesian method of estimating sex-specific von Bertalanffy growth parameters (DW_∞, k) in wild recaptured versus aquarium-housed rays. Additionally, we estimated growth from repeated measurement data collected from aquarium-housed rays, to obtain growth parameters while allowing for individual variability. Between 2009 and 2020, 590 whitespotted eagle rays were caught, measured, tagged and released along the southwest coast of Florida. Thirty-four were recaptured between 5–1413 days at liberty. Nineteen additional rays were collected, transported and maintained at Georgia Aquarium, Atlanta, with regular size and weight monitoring. Wild whitespotted eagle rays were found to grow faster and mature earlier than previously thought, with Bayesian estimates of k = 0.28 year-1 in females, and k = 0.30 year-1 in males. Aquarium-housed individuals seemed to grow slower and reach smaller sizes, although data provided by the aquariums showed variable growth patterns depending on the facility. Life history parameters and growth trajectories generated from this study offer valuable information to aid with future conservation management strategies of this endangered species.

title: Vulnerability of chondrichthyan fishes of the Eastern Tropical Pacific to climate change

authors.affiliation: Charles Darwin Foundation

abstract_text: Climate change is an environmental emergency threatening species and ecosystems globally and leading to a critical need to understand how marine species will be affected. Vulnerability assessments provide a framework to assess climate impacts combining species' exposure to a stressor, their sensitivity, and their capacity to adapt. We used an Integrated Risk Assessment to evaluate the vulnerability of 132 chondrichthyan species in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) to climate change and identified eight climate change factors most relevant for the region. The overall vulnerability for 23% of ETP chondrichthyans is High and 76% are Moderately vulnerable to climate change. Most of the Highly vulnerable species are batoids (77%), and most (90%) are coastal species or linked to coastal ecosystems through nurseries. Ocean warming, in combination with hypoxia and acidification, will have the most widespread effect on ETP chondrichthyans, but coastal species and those with reliance on coastal habitats will also contend with changes sea level rise and salinity from freshwater inputs. Vulnerability increases with synergies with other anthropogenic factors already occurring in the region, thus mitigating the impacts of climate change on ETP chondrichthyans include addressing issues with overfishing and habitat destruction too. Specific actions may be required for species at higher risk including protecting coastal bays and estuarine habitats, addressing fisheries sustainability, and reducing mortality. This assessment also identified knowledge gaps concerning ETP chondrichthyans and highlights the need of further understand the impacts of climate change on ETP habitats and processes.

abstract_text: In an increasingly stressed marine environment due to anthropic activities, the assessment of wildlife health becomes imperative. Marine organisms are exposed to a complex mix of pollutants which can compromise their wellbeing. Due to the life-history characteristics, use of habitats and distribution, Chondrichthyans are prone to bioaccumulate and biomagnify significant amounts of pollutants. Knowledge of immune and reproductive impairments on wild individuals can serve as an early alert of potential conservation threats. In this study we present preliminary results on immune and reproductive parameters of the elephant fish, Callorhinchus callorhynchus, inhabiting an anthropic impacted area. Elephant fish were captured by rod and reel from shore between October 2021 and April 2022, in the Golfo Nuevo, Chubut, Argentina. Hematological parameters and reproductive hormonal profiles are presented, constituting the first report for this species. Erythrocytes, thrombocytes and five types of leucocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes, heterophils, eosinophils and neutrophils) were characterized by light microscopy. Progesterone, estradiol and testosterone were measured in juveniles and adults of both sexes. This study provides baseline physiological information for the species, contributing to an ongoing research on the responses of the immune and reproductive systems within an ecotoxicological context.

abstract_text: As mid to upper trophic level predators, elasmobranchs are well known to have elevated levels of mercury and its more toxic, organic form methylmercury (MeHg). The lethality of methyl mercury across different taxa has been well researched, and its sub lethal effects have only been investigated in depth at the scope of human health with no focus on fish that have the highest mercury burden. However, the sub lethal effects of exposure to MeHg, which are known to impact animal behavior, cognitive ability, and physiology, remains largely undescribed. In this study, we establish baseline information on how the physiology of a small, coastal, demersal, elasmobranch species (Mustelis canis, smooth dogfish) is impacted by prolonged, sub lethal exposure of this widespread and potent contaminant. We assess sublethal effects of different levels of exposure using different physiological parameters including aerobic scope measured via oxygen consumption, growth rate, body condition, and food consumption. As a secondary objective we will use a novel approach where we assess cognitive impacts by measuring learning ability and memory through operant conditioning. Behaviors, such as foraging, prey capture, swimming behavior, memory, and learning are critical for many species of elasmobranchs yet are likely impacted by exposure to MeHg. Hence, assessing effects on physiology and behavior after sub-lethal exposure can give us an idea of how important physiological and cognitive processes may respond to changing ocean contaminant conditions.

abstract_text: Climate change and urbanization of coastal areas are impacting estuarine habitats globally. While these regions are important for the early-life development of many aquatic species, links between habitat use and foraging ecology are not well known. Thus, it is essential to understand the importance of threatened habitats for animals inhabiting estuaries to promote their conservation and improve ecosystem management. This study examined the importance of estuarine habitats as feeding grounds for juvenile bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) in the Clarence River, a nursery area where the species is targeted by commercial fisheries in New South Wales, Australia. Juvenile sharks (n = 54) ranging from one to ∼6.5 years-old, together with particulate matter and several primary producer species of mangrove and saltmarsh, were sampled for δ13C, δ15N and δ34S stable isotopes. Bayesian mixing models and a Generalized Additive Mixed Model were used to investigate the contribution of estuarine habitats to the diet of bull sharks and changes with growth. The importance of resources consumed from within mangrove habitats for juvenile bull shark resource use was minimal but slightly increased with age, with younger sharks (<2.5 years) relying on prey feeding on sources derived from particulate organic matter, while older juveniles (4–6.5 years) preyed on species that relied mostly on threatened saltmarsh habitats. Our findings highlight the important linkages between habitats of conservation concern and species redistribution in response to climate change, particularly as the animals could be moving towards new areas lacking suitable estuarine habitats.

abstract_text: The coastal marine stingray species Hypanus berthalutzae is endemic to Brazil and occurs south of the Amazon river mouth to São Paulo state, besides some oceanic islands and reefs. Until its description, H. berthalutzae specimens were identified as H. americanus and due to its recent recognition, few studies on the natural history of H. berthalutzae have been published using its current name. However, many previous studies were done with H. americanus: specimens now recognized as H. berthalutzae. To identify the existing knowledge on the natural history of this stingray, we surveyed online databases for studies accomplished with Brazilian specimens using a combination of keywords related to its location and species. A total of 123 searches returned 93 documents with information on H. berthalutzae. These were divided into 15 categories according to their research area, and the commonest ones were Ecology (33%) and Fisheries (24%). Overall, studies report larger females than males (TL/DW >75 vs. >51) and in a higher sex ratio (female:male, 21.3:1), with nursery areas in Rio Grande do Norte and Fernando de Noronha. Besides, H. berthalutzae represents approximately 5% of captured batoids in Southeastern Brazil when sequencing the mitochondrial maker COI, and occurs in depths varying from 0 to 77.5 m. However, we noticed a lack of studies concerning Reproduction, Physiology, and Evolution of this stingray, areas that should be the focus of future studies since it is already a Vulnerable species under the IUCN Red List assessment and is currently suffering from a high artisanal fishing pressure.

abstract_text: Manta rays have some of the lowest productivity rates of elasmobranchs and are threatened with extinction. Knowledge gaps in birth and growth rates, and habitats used by young persist. abstract_text: The longtail stingray Hypanus longus, is distributed from México to Ecuador. At present, it is the most commercially important ray in south of Mexico and Central America. The goal is to know the reproductive biology of this ray species in order to gather biological information for application into fisheries management plans. The morphometric data from 2659 organisms (1248 females, 1411 males) were obtained from January 2019 to February 2021. The females had an average size of 83.32 ± 22.34 cm disc width (DW) (41-178 cm DW); while in males the average size was 78.18 ± 10.46 cm DW (47-109 cm DW). There were no significant differences between the sizes of females and males (Mann-Whitney p=0.2768). The sexual ratio was 0.88H:1M (χ2=13.12; p<0.05), males were the most numerous group. In terms of reproductive parameters, 495 organisms (219 females and 276 males) were analyzed. The L50 was 105.42 cm DW for females and 75.73 cm DW for males. Both values are lower than the sizes previously reported for this species. Also using histology we found that mature males had fully developed sperm; whilst mature females developed uterine milk-secreting crypts in the trophonemata. The fecundity of females was 1 to 6 embryos. The sexual ratio of the embryos was 0.76H:1M, (χ2=0.83; p>0.05). This species have an asynchronous reproductive system. This is the first study about the reproductive biology on this species in Southern Mexico and the Central American Pacific.

abstract_text: Among luminous elasmobranchs, the kitefin shark, Dalatias licha, is a giant reaching up to 1.8 m. Here, through pharmacological and histological studies, bioluminescence of the largest luminous vertebrate is unveiled. Light organ (photophore) histology and bioluminescence control mechanisms are compared with known luminous elasmobranchs (Etmopterus species and S. aliae). Photophore histology revealed a conserved structure among the Dalatiidae family. Dalatiidae sharks harbor photophores constituted of a single photocyte (light emitting cell) encapsulated in a pigmented layer, surmounted by an iris-like structure (ILS) and topped by one or several lens cells. Etmopteridae photophores are more complex. They are composed of a black round shaped pigmented sheath encompassing group of photogenic cells, a lens formed by 2 to 3 lens cells, and an ILS formed by chromatophores. In parallel, a similar hormonal control of the light emission is highlighted. Melatonin triggers light production, while alpha-melanocyte stimulating and adrenocorticotropic hormones inhibit it. For both families, ILS pigment motion is involved in a mechanical regulation of the light emission. Recently, an extraocular opsin (encephalopsin) was also demonstrated as playing a role in the light emission control in Etmopteridae. The encephalopsin presence was recently described during the ontogenic development of the photophore from the dalatiid S. aliae. Hence leading to the search for D. licha extraocular opsin. By integrating the new data on the largest luminous vertebrate, D. licha, to previous researches, a comparative analysis will be conducted to highlight a clear bioluminescent structure and control mechanism conservation throughout evolution in luminous deep-sea sharks.

abstract_text: Despite being one of the most abundant pelagic and most wide ranging shark in the world, much still needs to be learnt about blue shark biology and ecology. As the most frequently fished oceanic shark, the population is reported to have declined by up to 70% in the Atlantic, which raises concerns about the future survival of the species. Life history parameters and knowledge of a species' ecology are key for management and conservation, particularly when the protection of larger areas is not feasible. In Irish waters, the population of blue sharks present during the late spring to early autumn is predominantly female but information about their reproductive status and feeding ecology during this time is lacking. Here, we integrate the results from sex steroid hormone analysis (progesterone and 17β-oestradiol) in blood plasma to assess reproductive status. In addition, using omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) in both plasma and muscle tissues, we investigate the effect of nutrition and diet strategies on the reproductive state of female blue sharks. We will also present data on hydrogen stable isotopes of PUFA to indicate the ability of blue sharks to perform endogenous conversion of dietary PUFA into important physiological omega-3 PUFA.

abstract_text: In behavioural ecology, interest in the study of animal personality (i.e. consistent individual differences in behaviour) has increased in the last two decades as it is believed to have important ecological and evolutionary consequences. These consequences are especially pronounced when personality covaries with other behaviours (i.e. behavioural syndrome) or with life-history (i.e. pace-of-life syndrome). So far, studies of personality on behavioural, and pace-of-life-syndromes have produced ambiguous outcomes, and the prominence of studies on captive animals in the literature may be a reason for inconclusive results. To address this knowledge gap, we tested personality in wild juvenile lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris) from 2012 to 2018 to investigate the emergence of behavioural and pace-of-life-syndromes under relevant ecological pressures. We first explored how to quantify meaningful personality traits in our study species. We then investigated (1) whether a behavioural syndrome existed between two consistent traits and whether the appearance of the syndrome was context dependent, (2) whether a growth-mortality trade-off was mediated by personality and (3) whether personality could predict the foraging habitat of sharks and whether this link was context-dependent. Overall, our research suggest that ecological conditions play a crucial role in the emergence and the shaping of personality and trait association. This work offers a possible explanation for the ambiguous results of previous studies and highlights the importance of increasing the focus on wild study systems in future animal personality research. Along with recent revisions of the personality research framework, this work may help paving the way for future shark-personality research.

abstract_text: Ongoing climate change is responsible for shifting the distribution of many marine species and may lead to changes in community structure and ecosystem functioning, especially where species perform unique functions such as elasmobranchs. However, this issue has been rarely studied in these species due to the limited amount of occurrence data and may have led to an underestimation of the underlying threats. It can be circumvented by identifying functional traits that explain range shifts in elasmobranchs rather than by studying individual species responses. Therefore, our aim was to detect and quantify distribution changes in demersal elasmobranchs in response to ocean acidification and increasing sea temperature and assess whether such changes can be attributed to their functional traits. To undertake this study, we collated scientific bottom trawl surveys data from 1997-2020 across the European continental shelf and employed a multispecies joint distribution model to model their habitat and understand potential variations in distribution with time according to sea water temperature and pH. The responses of trophic level, reproductive guild, preferred depth and latitudinal range traits according to these climate change variables were equally explored. From this analysis we highlight species whose range has shifted over the past two decades. Community structure variations are described over time and functional groups that are appear to be more vulnerable to future climate changes identified. Fishing pressure is also tested as a complementary factor affecting elasmobranch distribution over time
